claims.text: Single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys exhibit an exceptional combination of high strength and ductility during rapid loading.
Severe local lattice distortions with high mean-square atomic displacement provide strong solid-solution strengthening in single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortions increase resistance to dislocation glide.
Dynamic solute pinning and release prevents catastrophic dislocation pile-up.
Dynamic solute pinning and release promotes distributed plastic flow.
The combination of lattice-distortion strengthening and dynamic solute pinning enables elevated dynamic yield strength while retaining plastic deformation capacity.
Compositional complexity produces high mean-square atomic displacement and localized lattice distortions.
The localized lattice distortions form robust, spatially heterogeneous obstacles to dislocations.
The same lattice distortions facilitate dynamic solute pinning.
At moderate-to-high temperatures, thermally assisted solute diffusion causes transient dislocation pinning and release.
Transient solute pinning and release produces serrated flow.
Serrated flow caused by pinning and release delays strain localization and accommodates plastic deformation.
At very low temperatures, reduced phonon damping permits dislocation inertia to partially blunt the strengthening effect.
At higher temperatures, diffusion-assisted pinning predominates over the low-temperature inertial mechanism.
Relative to a simpler single-phase FCC alloy, the HEA will have higher dynamic yield strength across the tested strain-rate and temperature range.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the HEA will retain ductility and show more pronounced moderate serrated flow at elevated temperatures.
At cryogenic temperatures, the increase in HEA strength with decreasing temperature will become less steep because of dislocation inertia.
Dynamic solute pinning should be active roughly above 673 K.
The hypothesis is limited to single-phase chemically complex FCC alloys below temperatures where phase transformations or grain-boundary effects dominate.
Below approximately 60–77 K, dislocation inertia may modify the mechanical response.
